body.text: Dharmakīrtipraṇītā Santānāntarasiddhiḥ
body.translated_text: <s>Saṃtānāntarasiddhi</s> (Proof of Other Mind-Streams) composed by <s>Dharmakīrti</s>

children.translated_text: Having seen purposeful action (preceded by cognition) in one's own body, if from perceiving that same kind [of action] elsewhere,
mind is inferred—then even for the proponent of <s>cittamātra</s> (mind-only), this reasoning is the same.

body.text: ātmani cittaspandanapūrvau kriyābhilāpau dṛṣṭvānyatra tayordarśanādyadi spandanamanumīyeta, cittamātre 'pyaṣa nayaḥ samaḥ / ataḥ cittamātratāvādī api paracittamanumātuṃ śaknoti / tacca kāyavāgvijñaptipratibhāsi jñānaṃ jñānāntaraspandanaveśeṣeṇa vinā bhavatyevaṃ na matam / [1-3]
body.translated_text: Having seen in oneself that action and speech are preceded by mental impulse (<s>citta-spandana</s>), if from seeing those elsewhere one infers the impulse, even for the proponent of <s>cittamātra</s> (mere mind), this reasoning is the same. Therefore even a proponent of the <s>cittamātra</s> doctrine can infer another's mind. And the cognition that appears as bodily and verbal expression (<s>kāya-vāg-vijñapti</s>) does not arise without a particular impulse of another cognition—this is the accepted view. [1-3]

body.text: atha parajñānasya kriyānupalambhāt paradhīranumātuṃ na yujyata iti cet? na; tulyatvāt paro 'pi parajñānapūrvau tau kadāpi na paśyati 'taḥ tenāpi tanna jñāyate / [4-5]
body.translated_text: Now, if [it is objected that] it is not proper to infer another's mind because the actions [preceded by] another's cognition are not perceived—no, because of parity: the other too never sees those two [action and speech] as preceded by another's cognition; therefore by him too that [other's mind] is not known. [4-5]

body.text: ātmanaścittasya paravartinornimittatvānupapatteḥ paracittaṃ jñāyata iti cet / kiṃ na yujyate? svasamutthāpakacittasya pratisaṃvedanābhāvāt, ātmacittaśrayiṇoścātmani darśanāt / tāvapi yadi yathā syātāṃ tādṛśāvupalabhyeyātām / anyathā darśanādanyanimittaṃ sidhyatīti cet? aparasminnapi samānameva, svasamutthāpakacittasya saṃvedanābhāvāt / svacittaspandananimittake vijñaptipratibhāsinī jñāne cāntarmukhapratibhāsinī pratīteḥ bahirmukhapratibhāsinī anyanimittadutpadyete / [6-12]
body.translated_text: If [you say that] because one's own mind cannot function as the cause of what pertains to another, another's mind is known—what is improper [in our position]? Because there is no direct awareness of one's own mind that produces [those actions in others], and because the two [action and speech] that depend on one's own mind are seen in oneself. If those two were as you claim, they would be perceived as such. If [you say] from their being seen differently, another cause is established—the same applies in the other case as well, because there is no awareness of one's own mind that produces [the actions]. And in cognition that appears as expression (<s>vijñapti-pratibhāsin</s>), caused by one's own mental impulse, inward-appearing awareness arises; the outward-appearing ones arise from another cause. [6-12]

body.text: animitte eva bahirmukhapratibhāsinīti kinneṣyate cet? animittatve sarvasyānimittatvaṃ prasajyeta / vicchinnāvicchinnapratibhāsakṛto bhedo na jñānayoḥ spandanatvanimittabhedavibhāgakṛt / tenāvicchinnapratibhāsinorapyanimittatvaṃ bhavet, viśeṣābhāvāt / tathā sati, avicchinnatvaviśiṣṭaḥ pratibhāsabheda eva spandanapūrvako na bhavati / kintarhi? vicchinnasyāpi kriyāviśeṣasya pratibhāsa eva / śaropalaprakṣepaṇayantranirmāṇaparapracālanādikriyāviśeṣapratibhāsināṃ vicchinnasyāpi pratibhāsasya spandanapūrvakatvāt / parakṛtacālanādināṃ cāvicchinnasyāpyatadpūrvakatvāt / [13-19]
body.translated_text: If [you ask] why not accept that the outward-appearing ones are without any cause? If they were without cause, the absence of cause would apply to everything. The distinction between cognitions made by interrupted and uninterrupted appearance is not produced by the differentiation of cause based on whether there is an [internal] impulse or not. Therefore, even for uninterrupted-appearing cognitions, causelessness would follow, since there is no distinguishing feature. That being so, the difference of appearance characterized by uninterruptedness itself would not be preceded by [mental] impulse. What then? Even the appearance of a specific interrupted action would require explanation. Because for cognitions appearing as specific actions—shooting arrows, throwing stones, operating machines, moving others, and the like—even interrupted appearance is preceded by [mental] impulse. And because for being moved by another and the like, even uninterrupted appearance is not preceded by that [one's own impulse]. [13-19]

body.text: tena hyatra kriyāviśeṣamātreṇa spandanasya pratītiritī yujyate / tatra yadi kasyacidpūrvakatvam, na ko 'pi tatpūrvakaḥ syāt, viśeṣābhāvāt / ataḥ kriyāviśeṣasāmānyaṃ spandanaviśeṣasāmānyasya gamakam / tatra yathā kriyāmupalabhya, ātmani spandanānupalambhādanyatra spandanapratītiḥ; tathā kriyāpratibhāsopalambhane 'pi / samānametat; paro 'pi parakriyābhilāpayornimittaṃ nāstīti kinnecchati? tenāvaśyaṃ tau spandananimittakatvāt tadbhāve na bhavata iti vaktavyam / paro 'pi tayoḥ pratibhāsau tathaiva vadet / ataḥ nānayoḥ parasparaṃ bhedaḥ / [20-26]
body.translated_text: Therefore, here it is proper that the awareness of [mental] impulse is through specific action alone. There, if some [actions] were preceded by it, then none would be preceded by it, since there is no distinguishing feature. Therefore, the generality of specific action is indicative of the generality of specific [mental] impulse. There, just as, having perceived action, from the non-perception of [mental] impulse in oneself, there is awareness of impulse elsewhere—so too when the appearance of action is perceived. This is the same. Does not the other too hold that there is no cause for another's actions and speech? Therefore, since those two necessarily have mental impulse as their cause, one must say they do not exist without it. The other too would say the same regarding the appearances of those two. Therefore, between these two [positions] there is no mutual distinction. [20-26]

body.text: yadi tatra pratibhāsinyoḥ spandananimittakatvamucyate, svapnāvasthāyāmapi kinnocyate? sarva samānam / paro 'pi svapnopalabdhaparakriyābhilāpau spandananimittakāviti kinna vadati? tayorabhāvāditi cet / tathopalabdhisāpyāt kinna staḥ? atha middhenopahatatvāt puruṣasya arthaśūnyaṃ vijñānaṃ jāyata iti cet / paramate 'pi tasmādeva parādhipatyaśūnyaṃ vijñānamupajāyate / [27-32]
body.translated_text: If it is said that mental impulse is the cause of the appearing cognitions, then why is the same not said in the dream state? Everything is the same. Does not the other too refrain from saying that actions and speech of others perceived in dreams are caused by [another's] mental impulse? If [you say they are unreal] because of their non-existence—since they are perceived similarly, why are they not [real]? If [you say] because the person's consciousness, impaired by sleep, arises devoid of objects—in the other's [the <s>Yogācārin's</s>] view too, from that same cause, consciousness arises devoid of the control of another. [27-32]

body.text: atha svapne 'pi jñānasyārthavattvāttadopalabhyamānā api parasantānā eveti cet / paraṃ prativigrahītuṃ yadi yuktyāgamarahitastathāvidho 'sad vādaḥ samāśriyeta, tadā parābhimataṃ tasya parāyattatvaṃ na ko 'pi nivārayet / etatkeṣañcinmata eva sarvāṇi tathāvidhāni jñānāni santānāntarāyattāni / viṣeṣastu sākṣātparamparayā ca / kadācit svapne 'pi tasya sākṣāt santānāntarayattā iṣṭaiva; devādyadhiṣṭhānataḥ satyasvapnadarśanāt / tasmādasya naitadasadvādasamāśrayaḥ / [33-38]
body.translated_text: Objection: Even in dreams, since cognition has a real object, other mind-streams are inferred even though not directly apprehended. Reply: If, in order to refute the opponent, such an unsound thesis devoid of reasoning and scriptural authority were adopted, then no one could prevent the opponent's claim that it is dependent upon that other [mind]. According to the view of some, all such cognitions are indeed dependent on other mind-streams. But the distinction is between direct and indirect dependence. Sometimes even in dreams, direct dependence on another mind-stream is accepted, since veridical dreams are seen through the intervention of <s>devas</s> (gods) and others. Therefore, this is not for him an adoption of an unsound thesis. [33-38]

body.text: tāvattayā kriyayāpi taccittaṃ kathaṃ jñāyate? cittasya kāryatvāt / tasya kāryatvaṃ tu cittāntare 'pi tulyamiti kathanna jñāyate? api ca, yadi tatkriyā svasattāmātreṇa svasantānaṃ pratyāyet, tadānupalabhyamānenāpi syāttathā pratipattiḥ / na; jñānāpekṣatvālliṅgasya iti cet / tada tatra kimanayā paramparayā - paracittāt kriyā, kriyātaḥ jñānam, jñānāt tasya pratipattiriti / [39-44]
body.translated_text: First, how is another's mind known even through that action? Because it is the effect of mind. But if being an effect applies equally to another mind as well, how then is [the specific mind] not known? Moreover, if that action, by its mere existence, were to indicate its own mind-stream, then even when not apprehended, such a cognition would still arise. No, because the inferential mark is dependent on cognition. If so, then what need is there of this chain — from another's mind arises action, from action arises cognition, from cognition arises the ascertainment of that [mind]? [39-44]

body.text: paracittaprabhavadharmi kriyāpratibhāsijñānamevāsya gamakaṃ bhavati / tasyādhigatistu antaśaḥ tadāśritatvāt / spandanamātrasāmānyaṃ kriyābhilāpajñānasāmānyasya kāraṇatvāt kāryeṇa kāraṇasya gatiḥ / tatra ātmaspandananimittakasyāntarmukhavṛttiḥ, anyasyānyathā / prāyeṇādhikṛtyāsau bhedaḥ / etayoḥ saḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ svāpādyavasthāyāmitarasyāmapi ca samānaḥ / bhrāntyavasthāyāṃ yathāsvaṃ pratyayaviśeṣopāśrayāt paraspandanadinimittodbhūtavijñānavāsanaiva kadācitparābhogādeḥ vyavahitādapi vṛttiṃ labhate: na tvatyantāsadābhogāt / tasmāt sarvāvasthāsu kriyādivijñapteḥ cittaspandanamanumīyata eva / [45-51]
body.translated_text: The cognition in which action appears, having the property of originating from another's mind, is itself the means of knowing it. And the ascertainment of that [other mind] is at the very least because it [the cognition] is based on that. The general category of mere movement, being the cause of the general cognition expressed as 'action,' the cause is known through the effect. In this regard, cognition whose cause is one's own movement has an inward-directed function, while that of another is otherwise. For the most part, this distinction is with respect to the subject matter. The causal relation between these two is the same in the waking state as well as in the other [dream] state. In the state of delusion, depending on the particular conditions proper to each, the <s>vāsanā</s> (latent impression) produced by cognition arising from another's movement sometimes operates even from a remote experience of another's activity — but not from an experience that is entirely non-existent. Therefore, in all states, mental movement is indeed inferred from the communication of action and the like. [45-51]

body.text: kriyātaḥ spandanapratipattau svāpa itarasmiñca syātpratipattiratha vā naiva kadācana / paraspandanabhāve 'pi kriyālambanodayāt / bhavatvālambanodayaḥ, na tu kriyā / kriyayā spandanaṃ gamyate / bhrāntyavasthānāṃ kriyaiva na bhavati, arthaśūnyajñānodayānna doṣaḥ / sarvaprakāravyapadeśasāmyāt kadācijjñānamarthaśūnyam, anyadānyathā ityeṣo 'dhikāraḥ kuto labdhaḥ? atha middhādināvasthānyathābhāvaścet / yadyevaṃ sambhavet, bhavatu avidyopaplutatvāttathodayaḥ / tathā sati arthāntaravādahānyā ete 'nekāśakyanigūhanadoṣaprasaṅgāḥ mahākṛcchrā uttereṇaikena nihatā bhavanti / [52-58]
body.translated_text: If, from action, the ascertainment of [mental] movement follows, it should follow both in sleep and in the other state; otherwise it would never follow at all — because cognition taking action as its object arises even in the absence of another's [actual] movement. Granted, the object-based arising occurs, but not the action itself. Movement is known through action. In states of delusion, there is no action at all; since cognitions arise devoid of real objects, there is no fault. From the similarity of designation in all respects, the claim that sometimes cognition is devoid of a real object and at other times it is not — from where has this distinction been obtained? Objection: Because the state changes due to sleep and such conditions. Reply: If this be possible, let it be so — such arising occurs because of being obscured by <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance). That being the case, by the force of a single further argument, these difficulties — arising from the multitude of faults that cannot be concealed — entailing the fallacy of proving something other than what is intended, are all struck down with great difficulty. [52-58]

body.text: nanu tayoḥ darśanāt kāyavāgvijñaptibhyāṃ svamutthāpakacittasyānumānamiti nyāyyam / na tu santānāntarasambaddhavijñaptipratibhāsijñāne paravijñaptī bhavitumarhataḥ, tayoranupādānopādeyatvāditi cet / nocyate paracittasamutthitavijñaptirūpatvāttatra pratibhāsijñānena samutthāpakacittaṃ gamyata iti /
body.translated_text: Objection: Since both are observed, it is proper that from <s>kāyavijñapti</s> (bodily communication) and <s>vāgvijñapti</s> (verbal communication) the originating mind is inferred. But in a cognition in which the communications connected with another mind-stream appear, those communications of another cannot exist, because they are neither the material cause nor the material effect [of that cognition]. Reply: It is not said that by the cognition in which they appear, the originating mind is known because they are communications in the form arising from another's mind.

body.text: kiṃ tarhi? tasya kāryatvāt / vijñaptiriti samutthāpakacittasantānājjāte kriyāvāgākārake jñāne eva / samutthāpakacittaṃ ca tayorevopādānakāraṇam, santānāntarajñānayoḥ tvadhipatipratyayaḥ / vijñapterupādānātte janite / tatsambandhenopacārād vijñaptī bhavataḥ / bhavatu svaparayoḥ svasvapratibhāsasyānubhavaḥ, taimirikadvayadṛṣṭadvicandravat; tathāvidhavijñānasya hetuḥ vāsanotpādasvabhāvabiśeṣo 'nādikālikaikārthagrāhādhyavasāyitvāt / ekahetusambhūtayoḥ svaparavoijñaptijñānayoḥ vijñaptivenopacāraḥ / [59-64]
body.translated_text: What then? Because it is its effect. '<s>Vijñapti</s> (communication)' applies only to the cognition that arises from the mind-stream of the originator and has the form of action or speech. The originating mind is the material cause of those two [communications] alone, while for the cognitions in another mind-stream, it is the dominant condition (<s>adhipatipratyaya</s>). Since they are produced from the material cause of the <s>vijñapti</s>, they become <s>vijñaptis</s> by figurative usage through that connection. Let there be the experience of what appears to each in one's own and another's [cognition], like the two moons seen by two persons with cataracts. The cause of such cognition is a particular nature of the arising of <s>vāsanā</s> (latent impressions), since from beginningless time it has the character of grasping and determining a single object. The cognitions of one's own and another's <s>vijñapti</s>, arising from a single cause, are figuratively designated as <s>vijñaptis</s>. [59-64]

body.text: kiñca kriyādipratibhāsivijñānāt kāryaliṅgājjātaṃ yatparacittajñānaṃ tatparacittaṃ viṣayīkriyata āhosvinna? viṣayīkaraṇe 'rthāntaraṃ syāt / aviṣayatve tu kathaṃ jñānena paracittasattā pratīyate? tatsvarūpājñāne tatsiddhairasambhavāditi cet 3? eṣa prasaṅgo 'pi samaḥ / kriyāvāgbhyāṃ paracittaṃ pratipattimatāmapi tatsvarūpaviṣayīkaraṇe svacittajñānavat tadākārasyāpi jñānaṃ prasajyeta / tadajñāne tu tena tatsvarūpasya grahaṇaṃ katham? [65-67]
body.translated_text: Moreover, does the knowledge of another's mind (<s>paracittajñāna</s>), which arises from the inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>) of effect — from a cognition in which actions and so forth appear — take that other mind as its object, or does it not? If it takes it as an object, this would be something different [from what was intended]. But if it does not take it as an object, how is the existence of another's mind established by that cognition? [The opponent says:] Since, without knowledge of its intrinsic nature, its establishment is impossible. [Reply:] This objection applies equally [to the opponent]. Even for those who ascertain another's mind through actions and speech, if they take its intrinsic nature as an object, then knowledge of its form would follow, just as in the case of knowledge of one's own mind. But if that [intrinsic nature] is unknown, how can its intrinsic nature be grasped by that [inference]? [verses 65-67]

body.text: atha liṅgāt sāmānyadhigateḥ nākārasya pratītiriti cet? kiñca tatsāmānyaṃ paracittam evānyadvāhosvidavācyam / anyatvāvācyatvayorekatve tvanena tatsāmānyameva gṛhyeta, na paracittam / tatkathamanena tad gamyate? nāpi sāmānyaṃ paracittameva / tathā sati tadākārasyāpi jñānaṃ prasahyeta ityuktam / [86-71]
body.translated_text: If [the opponent says]: since through the inferential mark only the universal is ascertained, there is no cognition of the particular form — then what is that universal? Is it the other mind itself, or something else, or is it inexpressible? If otherness and inexpressibility amount to the same thing, then by this [inference] only that universal would be grasped, not the other mind. How then is that [other mind] known through this [inference]? Nor is the universal the other mind itself, for if it were so, knowledge of its form would also follow, as already stated. [verses 68-71]

body.text: na hyeṣā anumānaprakriyā / na hyanumānamarthasvarūpasya grāhakam / pratyakṣavat pratibhāsāviśiṣṭatvādeḥ prasaṅgāt / tena nāsya prāmāṇyam / tatsvarūpāgrahe 'pyabhipretārthāvisaṃvādāt prāmāṇyam / dhūmādiliṅgājjātamapi na vahnayādisvarūpaviṣayi, dṛṣṭenāviśeṣaprasaṅgāt / anumānasyātītādau niḥsvabhāvatāyā cāpravṛtteḥ, arthakriyāprasaṅgācca / [72-76]
body.translated_text: For this is not the procedure of inference (<s>anumāna</s>). Inference is not a grasper of the intrinsic nature of an object. Otherwise, there would be the unwanted consequence of its being no different from direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>), in terms of being indistinct in appearance, and so forth. Therefore, it would have no validity (<s>prāmāṇya</s>). [Reply:] Even without grasping the intrinsic nature, there is validity through non-deception (<s>avisaṃvāda</s>) regarding the intended object. Even [cognition] arising from inferential marks such as smoke does not take the intrinsic nature of fire and such as its object, because there would be the unwanted consequence of no difference from what is directly seen. And because inference does not operate regarding the absence of intrinsic nature in past [objects] and so forth, and because there would be the absurd consequence of [its producing] causal efficacy. [verses 72-76]

body.text: paracittānumāne 'pyabhipretārthāvisaṃvādo 'styeva / tatpravartanadvāreṇa prāṇyantarasattāṃ pratipadya punaḥ punarvyavahārapravṛttau tadādhipatyādāgārthasya prāpteḥ / tanmātraphalacintakasyalokasya prāṇyantarānumāne pravṛtteśca / uttarārthaviśeṣapratibhāsijñānānubhavodayamātreṇa puruṣasya nirākāṅkṣatvāt / pūrvajñānena vyavahārasamāpteḥ kṛtārthatatvaṃ pramāṇatvena siddhatvāt / [77-81]
body.translated_text: In the inference of another's mind too, there is indeed non-deception regarding the intended object. Through the medium of prompting action [in others], having ascertained the existence of another sentient being, in the repeated engagement in practical activity, the desired object is obtained through the dominance of that [other mind]. And because ordinary people, who consider only that much as the result, do engage in the inference of other sentient beings. And because a person becomes free from expectation merely through the arising of the experience of a subsequent cognition in which specific objects appear. And because the prior cognition's having accomplished its purpose — the completion of practical activity — is established as its validity (<s>pramāṇatva</s>). [verses 77-81]

body.text: nanu svapne 'pi pūrvajñānāduttarārthapratibhāsijñānamutpadyate / na tanmātreṇa pūrvajñānasya prāmāṇyaṃ yujyate, tadānīṃ sarveṣāṃ jñānānāṃ bhrāntatvāt / tatra vijñaptijñānaṃ na kadāciccittaspandanādhipatyena vinā udbhavatītyataḥ tābhyāṃ ye anumīyate / bhrāntivaśāt kadācid vyavahite 'pi udeti, na tu tadādhipatyarahitatvam / viśeṣastvasti sākṣātparamparayā cetyuktam / tatra yathā pūrvavijñaptijñānānāṃ paramparayā spandanādhipatyādudayaḥ tathā taduttarāvasthābhāvināmapi / vijñaptijñānāśrayaspandanottarāvasthācittasantānādeva paramparayotpādaḥ / tatrāpi yādṛganumānaṃ tādṛgavisaṃvādo vyavahāraścāpyastyeveti kenāpi na gṛhyate / [82-86]
body.translated_text: Objection: even in dreams, a subsequent cognition in which objects appear arises from the prior cognition. The validity of the prior cognition is not established merely by that, since at that time all cognitions are erroneous. [Reply:] In that case, a representational cognition (<s>vijñaptijñāna</s>) never arises without the dominance of a mental impulse (<s>cittaspandana</s>), and therefore the other mind is inferred from these two. Through the power of delusion, it sometimes arises even in a mediated [situation], but it is not thereby devoid of the dominance of that [mental impulse]. The distinction, however, exists between direct and indirect [causation], as has been stated. Just as the arising of the prior representational cognitions is through the indirect dominance of the [other's] mental impulse, so too is [the arising] of the subsequent states following those. The arising of the subsequent states of the mental continuum following the mental impulse that is the basis of the representational cognition is indeed through indirect [causation] from that very [other's] mental continuum. And in that case too, there is such inference, such non-deception, and such practical activity — this is not denied by anyone. [verses 82-86]

body.text: paracittānumānena tatsvarūpāgrahe 'pyavisaṃvādād bhavatu tathā prāmāṇyam / sākṣāt paracittavidāṃ tu katham? yadi te paracittasya svarūpaṃ sākṣājjānanti, tadā tasyārthāntaragrahaṇaṃ syāt / atha na jānanti, kathaṃ te sākṣādvidaḥ? kathaṃ nāma pratyakṣeṇārthasvarūpasya agrahaṇaṃ ca bhavati / atha na gṛhyate, kathaṃ tarhi pramāṇamiti cet? aprahīṇagrāhyagrāhaka vikalpayogināṃ paracittajñānamapi vyavahāre 'visaṃvādādeva pramāṇam, rūpādidarśanavat; āśrayāparāvṛteḥ / yogabalāddhi teṣāṃ jñānaṃ paracittākāraviśeṣānukāri sphuṭābhamupajāyate, karmadevādyadhiṣṭhānabalāt satyasvapnadarśanavat / teṣāmapi na paracittaviṣayitvena jñānamudeti, te 'pi tadākārasadṛśasvacittapratibhāsameva jānantītyevamavadhāraṇād paracittavida iti vyavahāraḥ / tadākārānukārisfuṭābhatvāt tatpratyakṣam, avisaṃvāditvācca pramāṇam iti matam / acintyo hi bhagavataḥ sarvārthādhigamaḥ, sarvathā jñānabhidhānaviṣayātītatvāt // [87-93]
body.translated_text: Through the inference of other minds (<s>paracittānumāna</s>), even without grasping the essential nature of those [other minds], let validity (<s>prāmāṇya</s>) be established in that way, since there is non-deception (<s>avisaṃvāda</s>). But how is it for those who directly know other minds? If they know the essential nature of another's mind directly, then there would be apprehension of something other [than one's own mind]. But if they do not know it, how are they direct knowers? How indeed could there be non-apprehension of the essential nature of an object by direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>)? And if it is not apprehended, how then is it a valid means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>)? — if one asks thus: For <s>yogins</s> who have not yet abandoned the conceptual distinction of apprehended and apprehender (<s>grāhya-grāhaka</s>), even their knowledge of other minds is a valid means of knowledge in conventional practice solely because of non-deception, just like the perception of form and so forth; because the transformation of the basis (<s>āśrayaparāvṛtti</s>) has not [yet] occurred. For by the power of <s>yoga</s>, their knowledge arises having a vivid appearance (<s>sphuṭābha</s>) that conforms to the particular aspects of other minds, like the perception of true dreams through the sustaining power of <s>karma</s>, deities, and the like. Even for them, knowledge does not arise as having other minds for its object; they too cognize only the appearance in their own mind that resembles the aspect of that [other mind] — it is precisely through this determination that the conventional designation 'knower of other minds' applies. Because of the vivid appearance conforming to the aspect of that [other mind], it is direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) of that, and because of non-deception it is a valid means of knowledge — such is the accepted view. For the Blessed One's (<s>Bhagavat's</s>) attainment of all objects of knowledge is inconceivable, since it utterly transcends the domain of all knowledge and expression.

body.text: // ācāryadharmakīrtipraṇītaṃ santānāntarasiddhiprakaraṇaṃ samāptam //
body.translated_text: The treatise <s>Saṃtānāntarasiddhi</s> (Proof of the Existence of Other Mental Continua), composed by the master <s>Dharmakīrti</s>, is completed.
